steps.en: The inferior vena cava is a bedside manometer for right atrial pressure. In a spontaneously breathing patient the cava collapses with the sniff driven fall in intrathoracic pressure, and the size of the vessel with the depth of that collapse maps to three pressure bands. The method takes under a minute with a subcostal window, works on a handheld probe, and anchors two bigger readings: the pulmonary pressure estimate and the fluid tolerance of a shocked patient. Learn it as a POCUS skill first and a laboratory number second.
Lay the probe subcostally in the long axis of the cava, showing it drain into the right atrium.
Measure the diameter 1 to 2 cm back from the atrial junction, avoiding the hepatic vein mouths.
Record M mode through the same spot during quiet breathing.
Ask for a brisk sniff and record the smallest diameter at peak collapse.
Compute collapse as the largest minus the smallest divided by the largest.
Read diameter with collapse together against the three pressure bands, and distrust the reading in ventilated or athletic patients.
Measuring an oblique slice of the cava. Fix: Slide until the cava and the atrial junction sit in one line. An oblique slice overreads diameter.
Measuring at the atrial mouth. Fix: The standard point is 1 to 2 cm back from the junction. At the mouth the number is falsely large.
Accepting a half hearted sniff. Fix: A weak sniff underreads collapse and overreads pressure, so coach a brisk sharp sniff.
Applying sniff bands to a ventilated patient. Fix: Positive pressure ventilation reverses the physiology, so do not apply sniff bands to ventilated patients.
Cava 21 mm or less with collapse above 50 percent. Right atrial pressure about 3 mmHg, range 0 to 5. Source: ASE right heart assessment, section on inferior vena cava and right atrial pressure
Cava above 21 mm with collapse below 50 percent. Right atrial pressure about 15 mmHg, range 10 to 20. Source: ASE right heart assessment, section on inferior vena cava and right atrial pressure
One criterion abnormal and the other normal. Right atrial pressure about 8 mmHg, range 5 to 10. Source: ASE right heart assessment, section on inferior vena cava and right atrial pressure

POCUS use of the same windows. Same diameter and collapse method at the bedside in shock and breathlessness protocols. Source: ACEP emergency ultrasound and international POCUS consensus, sections on volume status and venous congestion, in own words
Athletes carry wide cavas that still collapse fully; collapse rules over diameter.
Raised intra abdominal pressure squeezes the cava small despite high atrial pressure.
A fixed dilated cava with no collapse also appears in tamponade and tension physiology, so read it with the clinical picture.

q.en: Where is the caval diameter measured?

o.en: 1 to 2 cm back from the atrial junction
Beyond the diaphragm in the thorax

why.en: The standard point is 1 to 2 cm back from the right atrial junction, clear of the hepatic vein mouths, on a perpendicular cut.

q.en: A 24 mm cava with 20 percent collapse suggests which right atrial pressure?

why.en: A wide cava with poor collapse maps to the high band, about 15 mmHg with a range of 10 to 20.

q.en: Which finding fits a normal right atrial pressure?

o.en: Collapse above 50 percent with a 19 mm vessel
No collapse with a 26 mm vessel
Collapse of 10 percent with a 23 mm vessel
A vessel that grows with sniff

why.en: A 21 mm or smaller cava with collapse above 50 percent maps to about 3 mmHg, range 0 to 5.
